body.translated_text: First chapter: Establishment of Valid Cognition (<s>Pramāṇasiddhi</s>)

children.translated_text: To him whose profound and noble form is [revealed] through the dispelling of the web of conceptual constructions (<s>kalpanā</s>),
Homage to the one who is good in all ways (<s>Samantabhadra</s>), whose radiance pervades all directions. // 1.1 //
People are mostly attached to the ordinary; their understanding is weak — merely
surrounded by well-spoken words, they nevertheless hate [the teaching], stained by jealousy.

children.text: tenāyaṃ na paropakāra iti naścintāpi cetaściram sūktābhyāsavivardhitavyasanamityatrānubaddhaspṛham // Pramāṇav_1.2 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, this [work] is not for others' benefit — yet our mind has long been fastened [to it]: 'The passion nourished by the practice of good discourse [must be cultivated]' — with this aspiration firmly attached. // 1.2 //
Valid cognition (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is non-deceptive knowledge; [its] capacity for effective action (<s>arthakriyā</s>) is [its] mark.
Non-deceptiveness applies even to verbal [testimony], because it communicates the intention [of the speaker]. // 1.3 //
The meaning that appears in the mind through the activity of the speaker —
the validity of the word [lies] therein; it does not depend on the [ultimate] reality of the referent. // 1.4 //
Since [we do] not accept the validity of cognition as grasping what is [already] grasped, [but rather as] conventional (<s>sāṃvṛta</s>),
because activity is primary with regard to things to be rejected and adopted. // 1.5 //
And because of the difference in the aspects of the object [in cognition], and because of the difference in apprehension,

children.text: bhāvādevāsya tadbhāve svarūpasya svato gatiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.6 //
children.translated_text: when the entity exists, the knowledge of its own nature [proceeds] from itself. // 1.6 //
Validity [operates] in practical affairs; scripture serves to remove delusion,
or to illuminate what was previously unknown — [this is] beyond [mere] apprehension of [its own] nature. // 1.7 //
General knowledge is obtained when the particular (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) is unknown;
since the intention is 'that which is knowledge,' [we proceed] from the investigation of the particular. // 1.8 //
Similarly, the Blessed One (<s>Bhagavān</s>) is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid authority) for the cessation of what has [actually] come to be;

children.text: bhūtoktiḥ sādhanāpekṣā tato yuktā pramāṇatā // Pramāṇav_1.9 //
children.translated_text: [his] statement of what is real has [its] validity dependent on [establishing] the means [of liberation]. // 1.9 //
There is no eternal <s>pramāṇa</s>, since [things] existing [as real entities] are established by [valid] cognition;
because of the impermanence of the knowable, and because of the instability of sequentially-arising [cognitions]. // 1.10 //
Because of the impossibility of dependence [being related] to what arises separate from the eternal,
even in the impermanent, there would be non-validity — because of being in some way not beneficial. // 1.11 //
Non-activity after remaining [for a time]; specific configurations, effective action, and the like —
either the achievement of the desired [result], or non-achievement, or doubt regarding the example. // 1.12 //
What is established — [something] that has the continuity of the presence or absence of a governing agent of such-and-such a kind —
arrangement and the like that are consistent with that — therefore, what is inferred from that. // 1.13 //
When there is a difference in the real thing, from the similarity of words [applied] to what is non-different [in name],
inference is not justified — like [inferring] fire from the white substance [called 'pāṇḍu']. // 1.14 //
Otherwise, because a potter fashions a certain product of clay,

children.text: ghaṭādeḥ karaṇāt sidhyed valmīkasyāpi tatkṛtiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.15 //
children.translated_text: such as a pot — it would follow that an anthill too is made by him. // 1.15 //
Because the effect is accompanied by the proving property, even with a general [property] as the means of proof,
the fault of [asserting] difference because of difference in what is related — this is considered equivalent to [the fallacy of] the effect [reason]. // 1.16 //
From the observation of verbal similarity with what is established in another class (<s>jātyantara</s>),

children.text: na yuktaṃ sādhanaṃ gotvād vāgādīnāṃ viṣāṇavat // Pramāṇav_1.17 //
children.translated_text: it is not justified to use [universal] 'cow-ness' as a means of proving speech and the like — like a horn. // 1.17 //
Since words are dependent on the intention [of the speaker], there is no [fixed] place where words exist;

children.text: tadbhāvādarthasiddhau tu sarva sarvasya sidhyati // Pramāṇav_1.18 //
children.translated_text: but when that [intention] exists, in the establishment of meaning, everything would establish everything. // 1.18 //
By this, the doctrines of the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> (<s>Kāpila</s> and others) — such as the unconsciousness [of <s>Prakṛti</s>] — have been considered;
and [the view that] consciousness [arises] from what is impermanent [is refuted] — from death, by the method of exclusion (<s>apoha</s>). // 1.19 //
When the essential nature of the thing is established, this reasoning [applies]; when an attribute is established [for it],
[it is] non-contradictory — even when [the substrate is] unestablished, like sound [which some claim] rests on space. // 1.20 //
Even when [the substrate is] unestablished, the word succeeds when the thing is established;
just as the proof of form (<s>mūrti</s>) and the like [was offered] by a Buddhist (<s>Bauddha</s>) against the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> (<s>Aulūkya</s>). // 1.21 //
When that very [reason] deviates [from the thesis], even if the word does not deviate,

children.text: doṣavat sādhanaṃ jñeyaṃ vastuno vastusiddhitaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.22 //
children.translated_text: the means of proof should be known as faulty — [for the establishment of] a thing [depends] on the thing's [actual] establishment. // 1.22 //
Just as a thing is the cause of that [effect], so too it is the non-cause of that [same thing];

children.text: yadā tatkāraṇaṃ kena mataṃ neṣṭamakāraṇam // Pramāṇav_1.23 //
children.translated_text: when it is accepted as the cause of that, why is it not accepted as the non-cause? // 1.23 //
From the connection of <s>Caitra</s> with the sword and medicine, in the healing of a wound —

children.text: asambaddhasya kiṃ sthāṇoḥ kāraṇatvaṃ na kalpyate // Pramāṇav_1.24 //
children.translated_text: is causality not attributed to the post that is unconnected [with the healing]? // 1.24 //
Without a difference in intrinsic nature, activity too is not justified,
because the eternal [thing] is non-different [at all times]; and [its] capacity is difficult to establish. // 1.25 //
When those [causes] are present, [the effect] invariably arises; if one posits something other than those [as the cause],
[then one could posit] anything as the cause of anything — there would be no fixed determination of causes anywhere. // 1.26 //
The seed is the cause of the sprout's arising, through transformation of [its own] intrinsic nature;
earth and the like [serve as causes] of its refinement — because a specific [effect] of that [seed] is observed. // 1.27 //
Just as the aggregate of object, sense-organ, and the like — without a [further] distinguishing [factor] —
is the cause of cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), so too here — if not, [then it would follow that] there too, [cognition arises only] from a specific [additional factor]. // 1.28 //
When things that are individually incapable have no surplus [capacity] in their intrinsic nature,
even in combination there would be incapacity — therefore, surplus [capacity] is established from that [combination]. // 1.29 //
Therefore, among those things that are individually incapable but in which a quality is conceivable [in combination],
causality belongs to their combination — not to God (<s>Īśvara</s>) and the like, because of non-difference [of God from individual causes]. // 1.30 //
Validity is knowledge of a remote object; and because of the absence of a means [to verify such knowledge],
there is no [possibility of] practice — so some say. // 1.31 //
A knowledgeable person is sought for the understanding of what he has taught,
by those who suspect deception if an ignorant person gives instruction. // 1.32 //
Therefore, let the knowledge relating to what is to be practiced be examined;
of what use to us is the knowledge of the exact number of insects? // 1.33 //
He who is the knower of the reality of what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted, together with the means —

children.text: yaḥ pramāṇamasāviṣṭo na tu savasya vedakaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.34 //
children.translated_text: he is the desired <s>pramāṇa</s> (authority); but he need not be a knower of everything. // 1.34 //

children.text: dūraṃ paśyatu vā mā vā tattvamiṣṭaṃ tu paśyatu /
children.translated_text: Whether he sees far or not — let him see the reality that is desired;
if far-seeing were the criterion for being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, we would worship vultures. // 1.35 //
Compassion [is cultivated] through practice; that [compassion] depends on cognition, which depends on the body.
[Objection:] Practice [of compassion] is impossible [since the body is impermanent]. [Reply:] No — because of the refutation of [the need for a permanent] substrate. // 1.36 //
The arising of <s>prāṇa</s>, <s>apāna</s>, sense-organs, and cognition is not from the body alone,
if [we require that they arise] independent of [causes of] the same class — [in that case,] there would be birth [from the body alone, which is absurd]. // 1.37 //
[Objection:] From over-extension [of that reasoning], something unseen, possessing the power of reconnection,

children.text: kimāsīt tasya yannāsti paśyād yena na sandhimat // Pramāṇav_1.38 //
children.translated_text: must have existed [before] — what was that which [now] does not exist, by which [the person] does not reconnect [with a new body]? // 1.38 //

children.text: na sa kaścit pṛthivyāderaṃśo yatra na jantavaḥ /
children.translated_text: There is no portion of earth and the like where creatures —

children.text: saṃsvedajādyā jāyante sarva bījātmakaṃ tataḥ // Pramāṇav_1.39 //
children.translated_text: those born from moisture and the like — do not arise; therefore, everything is of the nature of a seed. // 1.39 //
In the arising of the sense-organs and the like, which do not require [a cause of] the same class,
just as one [element] transforms, so all [would transform] without distinction. // 1.40 //
Even when each [sense organ] is individually damaged, there is no damage to the mind — [yet this is the] view of [some];
when the mind is destroyed, the destruction of those [sense organs] is observed. // 1.41 //
Therefore, the substrate of cognition's continuity depends on cognition itself;
[there is] some cause of the sense-organs [that is itself cognitive]; therefore, the sense-organs [arise] from cognition. // 1.42 //
Whatever [cognition] previously impelled [the arising of the body], let it be of that same nature later too;
because of being benefited by the cognitions of that [body] — [thus] it is said that the mind depends on the body. // 1.43 //
Although cognition does not [arise] without the sense-organs, those [sense-organs] too [do not arise] without it;
nevertheless, [the claim of] mutual causation — [applies] even in the case of other mutually-causing [pairs]. // 1.44 //
A sequential [entity] does not arise from what is non-sequential; nor from what lacks distinguishing [features] when dependence is [posited];

children.text: kramād bhavantī dhīḥ kāyāt kramaṃ tasyāpi śaṃsati // Pramāṇav_1.45 //
children.translated_text: cognition arises sequentially from the body — [which] indicates the sequential [nature] of that [body-cause] as well. // 1.45 //
For something that is new at each moment, each preceding moment would be [the cause of] the preceding [moment];

children.text: tasya heturato heturdṛṣṭa evāstu sarvadā // Pramāṇav_1.46 //
children.translated_text: its cause — therefore let the cause always be just what is observed. // 1.46 //
What contradiction is there in the reconnection of another mind [in a new body]? [None.] Of the last consciousness [at death] —
even for the <s>Arhat</s>, from where is the reconnection of consciousness maintained? // 1.47 //
[Objection:] What purpose [is there] in following a doctrine with a <s>pramāṇa</s> whose object is unestablished?
[Reply:] If [you say it is] because of the deficiency of the reason — why then is that very [deficiency] not charged here [against your own position]? // 1.48 //
Like the cognition of that [thesis], although apprehension is possible, mental knowledge does not [arise] from the sense-organs;
because of the difference in the capacity to produce knowledge — not even from all [senses combined]. // 1.49 //
Because [matter] is unconscious, [consciousness does] not [arise] from another [i.e. material cause]; because of the non-difference of the cause, co-existence [would follow];
like the sense-organs, like form and taste — [consciousness] undergoes modification through the medium of the object. // 1.50 //
That which benefits existence, which is always connected with that [consciousness] —

children.text: sa hetuḥ saptamī tasmādutpādāditi cocyate // Pramāṇav_1.51 //
children.translated_text: that is the cause; therefore the locative [case is used, meaning] 'in [the body, consciousness arises]' — and it is also said 'from arising.' // 1.51 //
Let [the body] even be an assisting [cause] of the mind-continuum at some time,
like fire and the like [assisting the melting] of pots and the like — [still,] the cessation [of consciousness upon death] does not follow from that alone. // 1.52 //
[Objection:] There would be the unwanted consequence of non-cessation of consciousness while the body persists;

children.text: tadbhāvabhāvād vaśyatvāt prāṇāpānau tato na tat // Pramāṇav_1.53 //
children.translated_text: [Reply:] because [consciousness'] existence depends on the existence of that [body], and because of [its] being under [the body's] control — but <s>prāṇa</s> and <s>apāna</s> [show] this is not so. // 1.53 //
The impelling and drawing of the wind (<s>vāyu</s>) — from where [do they arise] without effort (<s>prayatna</s>)?
The decrease and increase [of breath] — from the decrease and increase of those [mental states]. // 1.54 //

children.text: tulyaḥ prasaṅgo 'pi tayoḥ na tulyaṃ cittakāraṇe /
children.translated_text: The same unwanted consequence [applies] to those two [breath and effort], but [it is] not equal regarding the cause of consciousness,
because another cause is accepted — one that [also] penetrates and sustains. // 1.55 //
[Objection:] If the body impaired by the <s>doṣas</s> (humoral imbalances) is not the cause, like a lamp-wick and the like,

children.text: mṛte śamīkṛte doṣe punarujjīvanaṃ bhavet // Pramāṇav_1.56 //
children.translated_text: [then] when the <s>doṣa</s> [causing death] is eliminated, revival should occur. // 1.56 //
[Reply:] Just as after fire is extinguished, the modifications of wood do not revert —
[so too] its non-reversion [is established]. [Objection:] Not so — because of the application of medical treatment. // 1.57 //
Some [modifications] are incapable of being restored [to their original state], yet produce [new] modifications;
some [are reversible] — just as fire [acts differently] on wood and gold. // 1.58 //
Of the first [irreversible type], even a small [modification] cannot be restored; but a modification that is produced [reversibly]

children.text: vikāraḥ syāt punarbhāvaḥ tasya hemnikharatvavat // Pramāṇav_1.59 //
children.translated_text: can be brought back — like the hardness of gold [which can be restored by heating]. // 1.59 //
Because of the difficulty of [finding] a restorer, some [conditions] are declared incurable;

children.text: āyuḥkṣayād vā doṣe tu kevale nāstyasādhyatā // Pramāṇav_1.60 //
children.translated_text: or because of the exhaustion of lifespan — but when the <s>doṣa</s> alone [is present], there is no incurability. // 1.60 //
[Objection:] A dead person, [if revived] by the removal of poison and the like, or even by severing [the bitten limb] —

children.text: vikārahetorvigame sa nocchavasiti sa nocchvasiti kiṃ punaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.61 //
children.translated_text: when the cause of the modification is removed — he does not breathe, he does not breathe! What more [need be said]? // 1.61 //
Without modifying the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>), the product (<s>upādeya</s>) cannot be modified —

children.text: kartu śakyāvikāreṇa mṛdaḥ kuṇḍādike yathā // Pramāṇav_1.62 //
children.translated_text: just as a pot and the like cannot be made without modifying the clay. // 1.62 //

children.text: avikṛtya hi yad vastu yaḥ padārtho vikāryate /
children.translated_text: For that thing which is modified into some entity without being itself modified —

children.text: upādānaṃ na tat tasya yuktaṃ gogavayādivat // Pramāṇav_1.63 //
children.translated_text: it is not proper [to call] that the material cause of that [product] — like a cow [cannot be the material cause] of a [wild ox] <s>gavaya</s> and the like. // 1.63 //
Thus, of consciousness and body — because of the arising of the effect from its [proper] cause —
their co-existence is due to cooperation, like fire and the melting of copper. // 1.64 //
[A substrate] is not the cause of persistence for either the existent or the non-existent, since [these] have no [need for a] substrate;
if the existent [had need of] a substrate — [then,] because of its non-difference from [the substrate's] persistence, [the substrate would be redundant]. // 1.65 //
Even in separation [from the substrate], it is [still] the cause of that [entity] — then what has the substrate done for the [entity's] existence?
[There would be] the unwanted consequence of non-destruction — if [the substrate] is considered the cause of destruction. // 1.66 //
The same unwanted consequence [applies] there too — what then [is the use] of a cause of persistence?

children.text: ā nāśakāgamāt sthānaṃ tataśced vastudharmatā // Pramāṇav_1.67 //
children.translated_text: If [you say] persistence [continues] until the arrival of a destroyer — then [persistence] is simply the nature of the thing. // 1.67 //
'The destroyer does not really obstruct [the thing]' — what [use] then [is] a cause of persistence?

children.text: yathā jalāderādhāra iti cet tulyamatra ca // Pramāṇav_1.68 //
children.translated_text: [Objection:] Like a container for water and the like? [Reply:] The same [argument applies] here too. // 1.68 //
For entities that perish at every moment, of the continuum of entities —
since arising likewise has a cause, a substrate is unjustified; otherwise [it would follow that nothing arises]. // 1.69 //
There may be a container for water and the like — [functioning] by obstructing [their] movement;
but what [use are] containers for immobile [things] — for qualities, universals, and actions? // 1.70 //
By this, <s>samavāya</s> (inherence), and inherent cause (<s>samavāyi kāraṇa</s>),
and the fixed existence of universals (<s>jāti</s>) and the like — [all these] are refuted, since they have no [need for a] substrate. // 1.71 //
[Objection:] If the destruction of entities [comes] from another [cause], what [is the use] of a cause of persistence for that [entity]?
It would perish even without those others — [since] the causes of persistence are powerless [to prevent destruction]. // 1.72 //

children.text: sthitimān nāśrayaḥ sarvaḥ sarvotpattai ca sāśrayaḥ /
children.translated_text: Not every persisting [entity] has a support, yet everything that arises has a support;

children.text: tasmāt sarvasya bhāvasya na vināśaḥ kadācana // Pramāṇav_1.73 //
children.translated_text: therefore, there is never destruction of any entity [on its own]. // 1.73 //

children.text: svayaṃ vinaśvarātmā cet tasya kaḥ sthāpakaḥ paraḥ /
children.translated_text: [Objection:] If [an entity] is itself of a perishable nature, what other [cause] could sustain it?

children.text: svayaṃ na naśvarātmā cet tasya kaḥ sthāpakaḥ paraḥ // Pramāṇav_1.74 //
children.translated_text: [Reply:] If [an entity] is itself not of a perishable nature, what other [cause] could sustain it? // 1.74 //
Even diminution and increase, [varying] according to differences in the operation of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>),
occur in wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>) and the like without [corresponding] diminution or increase of the body. // 1.75 //
This [feature] is not found in lamp-light and the like, which are dependent [on a support];

children.text: syāt tato 'pi viśeṣo 'sya na citte 'nupakāriṇa // Pramāṇav_1.76 //
children.translated_text: there would also be a distinction from those — but not in the case of a mind (<s>citta</s>) that does not assist [the body]. // 1.76 //
The increase of desire (<s>rāga</s>) and the like sometimes arises from nourishment and the like, [and sometimes] from pleasure and pain;
and [the increase] of those two [arises] from the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (<s>dhātu</s>), [and] from the proximity of an inner object. // 1.77 //
By this, loss of memory and the like [that arise] from conjunction [of bodily elements] are explained;
it is the intellect (<s>dhī</s>) itself that transforms [them], arising from particular inner objects. // 1.78 //
In [certain] lineages of tigers, [animals with] red [blood], and the like, where there is enhancement of the [mental] continuum,
delusion (<s>moha</s>) and the like arise — just as [they arise] from hearing and seeing. // 1.79 //
Therefore, [mind] invariably follows only its own mental impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>);
that [impression] is inseparable from mind (<s>citta</s>), and thus is dependent on mind. // 1.80 //
Just as a mental impression produced by hearing and the like, made in one mind, upon another mind,

children.text: kālena vyajyate 'bhedāt syād dehe 'pi tato guṇaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.81 //
children.translated_text: manifests over time — due to non-difference, that quality would [also] exist in the body. // 1.81 //
One who cannot be led by any other being, who grasps at a lower station,
who has attachment to self (<s>ātmasneha</s>), [does so] out of desire to abandon suffering and attain happiness. // 1.82 //

body.translated_text: Erroneous cognition regarding suffering, and craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) — these are the cause of bondage;

body.text: janmino yasya te na sto na sa janmādhigacchati // Pramāṇav_1.83 //
body.translated_text: one who does not have these two does not attain [re]birth. // 1.83 //

children.translated_text: [Objection:] If departure and arrival [of the mind] are not seen — [that is] because of the incapacity of the sense faculties (<s>indriya</s>);
[just as there is] non-perception by one with weak eyes of the movement of thin smoke. // 1.84 //
Due to subtlety, even something material may in some cases lack the capacity [to be perceived],
like water [pervading] or like thread in gold — [its] non-perception does not mean it is non-existent. // 1.85 //
When a hand and the like tremble, there would follow the trembling of everything [in the body] — which is contradictory;

children.text: ekasmin karmaṇo 'yogāt syāt pṛthak siddhiranyathā // Pramāṇav_1.86 //
children.translated_text: [if mind and body were one,] since a single action cannot [apply differently], there would be separate establishment otherwise. // 1.86 //
And when one [part] is obstructed, everything would be obstructed; [or] when not obstructed,

children.text: dṛśyeta rakte caikasmin rāgo 'raktasya vāgatiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.87 //
children.translated_text: when one [part] is colored [with passion], the passion of the non-colored [part] would be seen — or else there is no movement [at all]. // 1.87 //
There is no single aggregate because of this; and even in [the case of] multiplicity, [the problem is] as before;
due to non-distinction, and due to atomicity — if there is no movement, [perception] is not established. // 1.88 //
The non-distinction [applies] to those that are distinguished; being a sense faculty (<s>aindriyatva</s>) therefore [means] not being atomic;
by this, the absence of obstruction and the like is also refuted. // 1.89 //
And how [can one perceive] a mixture of thread, gold, and the like, or heated stones and the like?
How can the sense faculties (<s>akṣa</s>) and the like, which are individually incapable, have perception [of these]? // 1.90 //
[Objection:] If [perception arises] from conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) — then the same consequence applies to gold and thread;

children.text: dṛśyaḥ saṃyoga iti cet kuto 'dṛśyāśraye gatiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.91 //
children.translated_text: [reply:] If [you say] the conjunction is perceptible — how can there be perception in [something] whose support is imperceptible? // 1.91 //
And the connection of taste, form, and the like is conjunction only figuratively (<s>upacārataḥ</s>);

children.text: iṣṭaśced buddhibhedo 'stu paṃktirdirgheti vā katham // Pramāṇav_1.92 //
children.translated_text: if this is accepted, let there be difference in cognition — or how [can one say] 'the row is long'? // 1.92 //
Likewise, number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), conjunction, action, and the like — from their own nature,

children.text: abhilāpācca bhedena rūpaṃ buddhau na bhāsate // Pramāṇav_1.93 //
children.translated_text: and from verbal designation — form does not appear in cognition as different. // 1.93 //
In verbal cognition, through conceptual construction (<s>vikalpa</s>) that follows the distinctions in objects,

children.text: guṇādiṣviva kalpyārthe naṣṭājāteṣu vā yathā // Pramāṇav_1.94 //
children.translated_text: as in qualities and the like — [applied] to a constructed object, just as in [the case of] destroyed or not-yet-arisen [things]. // 1.94 //
If figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>) is accepted here, whatever is its basis,

children.text: sa eva sarvabhāveṣu hetuḥ ki neṣyate tayoḥ // Pramāṇav_1.95 //
children.translated_text: why is that very [basis] not accepted as the cause in all entities of those two? // 1.95 //
If figurative usage does not [apply] everywhere — [then you maintain] that the qualifier is different;

children.text: mukhyamityeva ca kuto 'bhinne bhinnārthateti cet // Pramāṇav_1.96 //
children.translated_text: [and that it is] the primary [meaning] — but why then does a different meaning [arise] in what is not different? // 1.96 //
Even if [they] do not cause a separate meaning, [terms like] 'white' and the like are not synonyms;
if words [applied to] that which possesses number and the like [denote] yet another meaning there too, // 1.97 //
there would be no distinction between quality (<s>guṇa</s>) and substance (<s>dravya</s>) — [they would be] different [only] due to difference in exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>);
even if [they have] the meaning of no separate entity, [they would function] like the word 'non-action' or 'non-substance'. // 1.98 //
And that which appears as if separate, indicated by words denoting entities,
and by words [denoting] that which possesses number and the like — that distinguishes [it] from other properties. // 1.99 //
The verbal testimony [of one who] desires to know only that [thing], not implying everything else,

children.text: bhinnaṃ dharmamivācaṣṭe yogo 'ṅgulyā iti kvacit // Pramāṇav_1.100 //
children.translated_text: indicates as if a separate property — 'connection with a finger,' for instance, in some [cases]. // 1.100 //
'Having a joined finger' — since it implies all [properties], it expresses the property-bearer;
even in denoting a well-known single meaning, it is similarly established in convention. // 1.101 //
[The word 'pot'] functions without implying the distinctions of capacities such as form and the like;
the word 'pot' (<s>ghaṭa</s>) [serves] to exclude [things that are] not causes having the same effect as that. // 1.102 //

children.text: ato na rūpaṃ ghaṭa ityekādhikararaṇa śrutiḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the statement 'form is a pot' is not a co-referential expression (<s>ekādhikaraṇa</s>);
this is the difference between [words] denoting a universal (<s>jāti</s>) and [words] denoting an aggregate (<s>samudāya</s>). // 1.103 //
'Form and the like of the pot' — these indicate the particular capacities of that [pot], subordinate to its generality;
other [things] too can be explained by this method. // 1.104 //
And when all [factors] together are the cause, even if one component is deficient, [the effect does] not [arise];
even if each individually has capacity, many [effects] would arise simultaneously. // 1.105 //
Not [so], because of the equality of multiplicity; <s>prāṇa</s> (inhalation) and <s>apāna</s> (exhalation) are the regulators;
even in [the case of] oneness, the manifold manifestation of that [mind] — because its cause is always present. // 1.106 //
[Objection:] If [you say] there is not a multiplicity of causes — [reply:] that is not so, due to non-distinction; and also because of sequence;
even when there is a single <s>prāṇa</s>, since multiple objects are grasped, the restriction [follows] from that. // 1.107 //
Let the cognition of many [objects] by one [mind] occur just once;
since there is no contradiction, [let it occur] also in sequence — let it not be [otherwise], due to non-distinction. // 1.108 //
If the many momentary <s>prāṇas</s>, which have no [gap of] time between those of the same class,

children.text: tādṛśāmeva cittānāṃ kalpyante yadi kāraṇam // Pramāṇav_1.109 //
children.translated_text: are postulated as the cause of precisely such minds (<s>citta</s>), // 1.109 //

children.text: kramavantaḥ kathaṃ te syuḥ kramavaddhetunā vinā /
children.translated_text: how can they have sequence without a cause that has sequence?
If [each] has its own prior [moment of the] same class as cause, the first one would not be possible. // 1.110 //
Such a cause for that does not exist; or if it does, multiplicity [of minds] is certain,
since the <s>prāṇas</s> are in different locations — therefore the simultaneous arising of cognitions is unacceptable. // 1.111 //
If many [prāṇas] existing at one time are the cause of a single consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>),
then even if one [prāṇa] is deficient, [consciousness should arise] — as in the case of shallow breathing and the like. // 1.112 //
Now, if the cause [produces effects] according to its [own] condition, then in cognition too there would be differentiation;

children.text: na hi tat tasya kārya yad yasya bhedānnna bhidyate // Pramāṇav_1.113 //
children.translated_text: for that is not the effect of that [cause] which is not differentiated when [the cause] is differentiated. // 1.113 //
<s>Vijñāna</s> (consciousness), due to the restriction of capacity, is a single [consciousness as] cause of a single [object];
and because [there is] no grasping of another object when cognition is impaired in its capacity for another object. // 1.114 //
The intellect (<s>dhī</s>), having arisen from the body all at once, is regulated by its own class;

children.text: parataścet samarthasya dehasya viratiḥ kutaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.115 //
children.translated_text: if [it is regulated] by another — then why does the capable body cease? // 1.115 //
Without a support, when the body ceases, the mind (<s>cetas</s>) would [also] cease to exist;
[objection:] '[it exists] in isolation' — if so, [then you must explain] the cause of the continuity of the mind-stream (<s>cittasantāna</s>). // 1.116 //
If [the body] does not serve as a component for obtaining the operation of that [mind's] cause,
[then] the cause of arising in another body is the five sense-bases (<s>pañcāyatana</s>) of this life. // 1.117 //
In denying that [the body] is the cause of being a component of that [mind], non-apprehension
is said to be inconclusive — [for] sense faculties and the like are also like the remainder. // 1.118 //
And the capacity of the previous sense faculties (<s>indriya</s>) in their own classes is observed;
from the observation of transformation, successive rebirth is also established. // 1.119 //

children.text: śarīrād yadi tajjanma prasaṅgaḥ pūrvavad bhavet /
children.translated_text: If that [mind's] birth is from the body, the same consequence as before would follow;

children.text: cittāccet tata evāstu janma dehāntarasya ca // Pramāṇav_1.120 //
children.translated_text: if [it is] from mind (<s>citta</s>), then let the birth of another body also be from that [mind] itself. // 1.120 //
Therefore, it is not the case that, due to deficiency of cause, [there is] a discontinuity for all final moments of mind;

children.text: asandhirīdṛśaṃ tena śeṣavat sādhanaṃ matam // Pramāṇav_1.121 //
children.translated_text: thus, [the continuity of mind] is considered to be established like the remainder. // 1.121 //
Even regarding the special [development] through practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) — like jumping, water, and heat —

children.text: svabhāvātikramo mā bhūditi ced āhitaḥ sa cet // Pramāṇav_1.122 //
children.translated_text: [objection:] 'let there not be a transcendence of [one's] nature' — if that [nature] is [already] established, // 1.122 //
if it again requires effort, it would have an unstable basis;

children.text: viśeṣo naiva vardheta svabhāvaśca na tādṛśaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.123 //
children.translated_text: the special [quality] would never increase, and such is not [its] nature. // 1.123 //
Since the capacities employed there [are directed] toward further special [developments],
due to the inability of the means [to produce results beyond them], and because there is never persistence without a support, // 1.124 //
since the special [quality] is not [something with] a fixed nature — even when established in growth,

children.text: nāpekṣeta punaryatnaṃ yatno 'nyaḥ syād viśeṣakṛt // Pramāṇav_1.125 //
children.translated_text: if it does not again require effort, [then] another effort would produce the special [quality]. // 1.125 //
Just as [the transformation] of wood, mercury, gold, and the like by fire and the like —
so compassion (<s>kṛpā</s>) and the like, born of practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>), proceed spontaneously (<s>svarasena</s>). // 1.126 //

children.text: tasmāt sa teṣāmutpannaḥ svabhāvo jāyate guṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, that quality which has arisen as their nature is born [from practice];
each successive effort is the producer of the special [development]. // 1.127 //
And since cognitions of compassion (<s>kṛpā</s>) and the like grow from prior seeds of the same class,
when practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is present, how could there be a limit to them? // 1.128 //
And it is not the case that jumping [leads] merely to [more] jumping; because of strength and effort,
which are its causes, having a fixed capacity — jumping has a fixed nature. // 1.129 //
At first, [jumping is limited] due to the deficiency of the body; later, as with non-jumping,

children.text: śanairyatnena vaiguṇye niraste svabale sthitiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.130 //
children.translated_text: gradually, through effort, when the deficiency is removed, there is stability in [one's] own strength. // 1.130 //
Compassion (<s>kṛpā</s>), arising from its own seeds, if it is not
obstructed by opposing [factors] born from their own seeds, attains absolute identity with the mind (<s>citta</s>). // 1.131 //

children.text: tathā hi mūlamabhyāsaḥ pūrvaḥ pūrvaḥ parasya tu /
children.translated_text: For thus, practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is the root — each earlier [stage serves as root] for the next —
for the refinement of compassion (<s>kṛpā</s>), detachment (<s>vairāgya</s>), insight (<s>bodha</s>), and the like, which are qualities of mind (<s>citta</s>). // 1.132 //
Through practice, [the mind] becomes of the nature of compassion — like aversion, detachment, and passion;
the supreme development of compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), produced [thus], is aroused by the suffering of others. // 1.133 //
The compassionate one engages in the means for the removal of suffering;
but the declaration of [things that are] beyond perception — the goal and its causes — is indeed difficult. // 1.134 //
Investigating through reasoning (<s>yukti</s>) and scripture (<s>āgama</s>), [the compassionate one] examines the cause of suffering;
and [examines] its nature of impermanence (<s>anitya</s>) and the like, through the qualifiers of suffering itself. // 1.135 //

children.text: yatastathā sthite hetau nivṛttirne ti paśyati /
children.translated_text: Since, when the cause remains in that state, [the compassionate one] sees that there is no cessation
of the result — for the purpose of removing the cause, [one] examines its opposite. // 1.136 //
The opposite of the cause is established through the understanding of the nature of <s>apoha</s> (exclusion);
the attachment (<s>sneha</s>) produced by the grasping of self (<s>ātman</s>) and mine (<s>ātmīya</s>), whose domain is mental impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), // 1.137 //
is the cause; the opposing [factor] — the vision of selflessness (<s>nairātmyadarśana</s>) — is its antidote;

children.text: bahuśo bahudhopāyaṃ kālena bahunāsya ca // Pramāṇav_1.138 //
children.translated_text: through many methods, in many ways, and over a long period of time, // 1.138 //
as one practices in that [vision], the virtues and faults become manifest;
and through the refinement of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), [the afflictive] latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) of the cause are abandoned. // 1.139 //
The distinction of the Great Sage from <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> and the like who act for others' [benefit] is this:
this very practice of the means [constitutes his path]; his teaching (<s>śāsana</s>) is considered [to serve] that purpose. // 1.140 //
Prior to completion, these two — the [noble] state and its cause — have been stated;
the threefold abandonment of the cause [constitutes] <s>Sugata</s>-hood (the state of the Well-Gone One), because of the absence of remainder. // 1.149 //
The excellence of the vision of selflessness (<s>nairātmyadṛṣṭi</s>) for [removing] suffering, or even through reasoning —
[when it is said that there is] no return — [this] has been stated [in relation to] birth, and the arising of faults. // 1.142 //
Through the abandonment of the seed of self-perception (<s>ātmadarśana</s>), there is no return;
because of [the realization of] a nature distinct from entities — the remainder is free from affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) and fever. // 1.143 //
Deficiency of body, speech, and intellect, or even lack of skill in teaching the path —
complete removal [comes] through practice; the diminishment of faults in speech and the like [follows]. // 1.144 //
[Objection:] 'No,' say some — the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>) of this is doubtful, because it is deviant (<s>vyabhicārin</s>);
and the inexhaustibility of faults [follows] from [their being] permanent, [or] from the absence of means [to remove them]. // 1.145 //
Or [one might] imagine [this] from the non-comprehension of the means [for removing faults].
Because the opposing [affliction] has a cause, and because [that] cause is destroyed through repeated practice,
through knowledge of the nature of the cause, knowledge of that [cessation] is also established.

children.text: tāyaḥ svadṛṣṭamārgoktiḥ vaiphalyād vakti nānṛtam // Pramāṇav_1.147 //
children.translated_text: The <s>Tāyin</s> (Protector, i.e., the Buddha) teaches the path he himself has seen; he does not speak falsely, because [doing so] would be fruitless.
And [his teaching is] for the benefit of others, due to his compassionate nature, and because he engages in all endeavors [for others].

children.text: tasmāt pramāṇam tāyo vā catuḥsatyaprakāśanam // Pramāṇav_1.148 //
children.translated_text: Therefore the <s>Tāyin</s> is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid authority), or [rather] his illumination of the <s>catuḥsatya</s> (Four Noble Truths) [is the pramāṇa].
<s>Duḥkha</s> (suffering) consists of the <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) of one in <s>saṃsāra</s>; from observing the intensification of <s>rāga</s> (desire) and the like,
[it arises] from habituation, not randomly, since arising without a cause is contradictory.
It is not a property of <s>vāta</s> (wind) and such [elements], because of deviation [from invariable concomitance], and because of the mixing of natures.

children.text: adoṣaścettadanyo 'pi dharmaḥ kiṃ tasya nekṣyate // Pramāṇav_1.150 //
children.translated_text: If it is not a defect, then why is that other property of it not observed?
Not every property belongs to all [beings]—there would be the absurd consequence of equal desire in all.
If [you say it is] not a defect, like form and such [qualities], the same objection applies there too.

children.text: ādhipatyaṃ viśiṣṭānāṃ yadi tatra na karmaṇām /
children.translated_text: If particular <s>karmas</s> (actions) do not have dominance in that [matter],
then even in the differentiation of the afflictions, because of non-differentiation, [your thesis] is unestablished.

children.text: na vikārād vikāreṇa sarveṣām na ca sarvajāḥ /
children.translated_text: Not all [beings experience] transformation through [every] transformation, nor do all [afflictions] arise from all [causes];

children.text: kāraṇe vardhamāne ca kāryahānirna yujyate // Pramāṇav_1.153 //
children.translated_text: and when the cause increases, a decrease in the effect is not logically possible.
The transformation of <s>rāga</s> (desire) and the like, as in [cases of] fever and such, is also born from pleasure and the like.
If <s>rāga</s> does not arise from suffering born of imbalance,
then one must explain: from what does it arise? From balance comes intoxication, and from that comes erotic desire.

children.text: rāgī viṣamadoṣo 'pi dṛṣṭaḥ sāmye 'pi nāparaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.155 //
children.translated_text: One who is desirous is seen to have the defect of imbalance, but another [without desire] is not [so seen] even in a state of balance.
Others too, from the diminishing of blood [i.e., vitality], weep; and intoxication is not fixed on a single woman.

children.text: tenaikasyāṃ na tīvraḥ syād aṅga rūpādyapīti cet // Pramāṇav_1.156 //
children.translated_text: If [you say] therefore it would not be intense toward one [woman], and that limbs, form, and such [are also factors]—
there is no invariable rule for all [in this regard], nor would it be indeterminate;

children.text: aguṇagrāhiṇo 'pi syāt aṅgaṃ so 'pi guṇagrahaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.157 //
children.translated_text: even one who does not apprehend qualities would have it [as] a factor—[but] that [desire] too is an apprehension of qualities.
If everyone were an apprehender of qualities, then because of non-differentiation of the cause,

children.text: yadavastho mato rāgī na dveṣī syācca tādṛśaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.158 //
children.translated_text: one who is in whatever state [and] considered desirous should not also be averse in that same [state].
Because the two [desire and aversion] are not of the same form, no fixed rule is observed here.
Their operations are bound to differences in <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions) of the same class.
For the one who has <s>rāga</s> (desire) and the like, these are not invariably concomitant defects.

children.text: etena bhūtadharmatvaṃ niṣiddham niḥśrayasya ca // Pramāṇav_1.160 //
children.translated_text: By this, [their] being essential properties (<s>bhūtadharma</s>) is refuted, and [the possibility of] liberation is also [established].
From the refutation [that they are essential properties], whiteness and such do not inhere in earth and the like [in the same way afflictions do not inhere in mind].
The word 'dependent upon that' has the meaning of [being related to] a cause, and [is understood] through its substrate.
Or [one might say] the substrate of form and such is [the same as the afflictions'] because they exist inseparably.

children.text: madādiśakteriva ced vinirbhāgaḥ na vastunaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.162 //
children.translated_text: If, like the power of intoxication and such, there is no separation from the substance,
[then] if the power were a separate entity, it would perish when [the power] does not inhere in the substrate;

children.text: tiṣṭhatyavikale yāti tattulyaṃ cenna bhedataḥ // Pramāṇav_1.163 //
children.translated_text: when [the substrate] remains intact, [the power] departs—if [you say] that is the same [as our case], [we reply:] no, because of the difference.
Because the cognitions of matter (<s>bhūta</s>) and consciousness (<s>cetana</s>) have distinct appearances,
up to the transformation of the body, the mind would have the same form [as the body—but this is not observed].
Like form and such, what dependence on objects does conceptual construction have?
When, without depending on the body, <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impressions) are the cause of cognition,

children.text: jñānaṃ syāt kasyacit kiñcit kutaścit tena kiñcina /
children.translated_text: a certain cognition arises for someone, of something, from something, by means of something.
This is established because what is not consciousness does not serve as the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) of consciousness.
If [you say] this is accepted because of the connection of consciousness with the power [in all things]—
what other self-respecting person would wish to say this, [which is the view] of the beast of <s>Sāṃkhya</s>?
'Something never before seen exists'—[this is like claiming] a hundred elephants on a blade of grass.

children.text: yad rūpaṃ dṛśyatāṃ yātaṃ tad rūpaṃ prāṅ na dṛśyate // Pramāṇav_1.168 //
children.translated_text: That form which has come into visibility was not visible before.

children.text: śatadhā viprakīrṇe 'pi hetau tad vidyate katham /
children.translated_text: Even when the cause is scattered in a hundred ways, how does that [form] exist [in it]?
The absurd consequence of non-determination of <s>rāga</s> (desire) and the like follows upon [the theory of] unprecedented manifestation.
If everyone has <s>rāga</s> and the like because they do not transcend the nature of the elements,

children.text: sarvaḥ samānarāgaḥ syād bhūtātiśayato na cet // Pramāṇav_1.170 //
children.translated_text: then everyone would have equal desire; and [if you say] not, because of the gradations of the elements—
even though there is no difference in the life-force of the elements, the difference [in desire] has this [element] as its basis;
like the decrease and increase of that [life-force], those [afflictions] should be eliminated through its [elimination].
If [you say] even in the difference [of elements], the causes of <s>rāga</s> and the like are not destroyed because of the sameness of their elemental nature,
then <s>rāga</s> would be equal everywhere, since the cause has the same nature.
For the cognition of a cow, there is nowhere [an instance] arising from the same nature [as the elements];
nor is there gradation in earth and such [that accounts for] sentience and the like, even here.
Even though there are gradations of heat, fire is never non-hot.
If [you say] it is likewise here—no, because [we] refute the difference [of affliction] from the heat of fire.
For one who has other qualities that experience gradation,

children.text: te kvacit pratihanyante tadbhede dhavalādivat // Pramāṇav_1.175 //
children.translated_text: those [qualities] are sometimes obstructed—in the difference of that [substrate], like whiteness and such.
As with form and the like, there is no fixed rule for those [afflictions], because the elements are undifferentiated.

children.text: tat tulyaṃ cenna rāgādeḥ sahotpattiprasaṅgataḥ // Pramāṇav_1.176 //
children.translated_text: If [you say] that is the same [objection]—no, because of the absurd consequence that <s>rāga</s> and the like would arise simultaneously [with all cognition].
And because objects are not the domain of conceptual construction, objects are not the determining factors.
Either there is no determination of <s>rāga</s> and the like because of the absence of a homogeneous cause,
or all cognitions would arise at all times, because of the proximity of the cause.
Because it is sometimes apprehended, that [affliction] is unstable; from the dependence on defects [we know this].
<s>Duḥkha</s> (suffering) [arises] because of being subject to causes; and it is neither the <s>ātman</s> (self), nor is it governed [by a self].

children.text: nākāraṇamadhiṣṭhātā nityaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ katham // Pramāṇav_1.179 //
children.translated_text: What is not a cause cannot be a governor; and how could a permanent [entity] be a cause?
Therefore, multiple [effects] do not arise from a single [cause] at different times.
From the non-arising of the effect when other causes are also present,
there would be inference of another cause; this does not exist in [the case of] permanent [entities].
Through [its] occasional [occurrence], the causedness of this suffering is established.
[A permanent entity would have] permanent existence or non-existence, because of not depending on external [factors] for [its] cause.

children.text: taikṣṇyādīnāṃ yathā nāsti kāraṇaṃ kaṇṭakādiṣu // Pramāṇav_1.182 //
children.translated_text: Just as sharpness and such in thorns and the like have no [external] cause,

children.text: tathā kāraṇametat syād iti kecit pracakṣate /
children.translated_text: so too this would be a cause—thus some declare.

children.text: satyeva yasmin yajjanma vikāre vāpi vikriyā // Pramāṇav_1.183 //
children.translated_text: [But we say:] that in whose presence something arises, or in [whose] modification a change [occurs],

children.text: tat tasya kāraṇaṃ prāhustat teṣāmapi vidyate /
children.translated_text: that they call the cause of that; and that exists for those [thorns] too.
Because touch is caused by form [i.e., material configuration], there is a causal basis in [its] manifestation.
By the refutation of permanent [entities], the possibility of <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and such is also [denied].
Because of [their] incapacity, therefore the cause [of suffering] is the grasping of the desire for existence (<s>bhava-tṛṣṇā</s>).
Because [the desire] of people for a particular place is produced by the hope of obtaining that,
that activity of one who desires attainment or non-attainment of existence would be [directed toward] pleasure and pain.

children.text: yato 'pi prāṇinaḥ kāmavibhavecche ca ta mate /
children.translated_text: Moreover, since living beings are considered to have desire for <s>kāma</s> (sensual pleasure) and <s>vibhava</s> (prosperity),
and because self-love (<s>ātmasneha</s>) is the cause everywhere, it operates [universally].
Of one who perceives pleasure in what is not pleasurable—therefore <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving) is the basis of existence.
Because of the observation that those free from desire are not reborn—thus the <s>Ācāryas</s> (Masters) teach.
From the observation that without desire for the body there is no [rebirth], and desire arises from the body,
the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>) is indicated by the approach of the proximate condition, but [the opponent's view] is refuted.

children.text: imāṃ tu yuktimanvicchan vādhate svamataṃ svayam /
children.translated_text: But one who seeks this reasoning himself contradicts his own position.
If [you say desire is] coexistent with birth, because desire is observed in the newborn—
the establishment of a homogeneous birth [as its cause] comes first; even regarding causation, [our position] is not challenged.

children.text: ajñānam uktā tṛṣṇaiva santānapreraṇād bhave // Pramāṇav_1.191 //
children.translated_text: Ignorance is said to be craving itself, because it impels the [mental] continuum toward existence.
And because of [its] immediate succession, <s>karma</s> (action) too, when that [craving] exists, cannot [independently] arise.
That [karma] is not ultimate, because of the possibility of obstruction and the like of [its] cause.
[The objection:] because of being a <s>saṃsārin</s>, there is no liberation—[this is] not established, because [liberation] is not desired [to be impossible].

children.text: yāvaccātmani na premṇo hāniḥ sa paritasyati // Pramāṇav_1.193 //
children.translated_text: As long as there is no diminishment of love for the self, one remains tormented.
For that long, projecting [the notion of] 'sufferer' [onto the self], one does not remain at ease.
The effort to remove false superimposition [is valid] even without [an already existing] liberated person.
The state of those free from desire (<s>vītarāga</s>), whether through compassion or through <s>karma</s>,
when [karma] is projected but there is no wish for non-cessation—through the exhaustion of cooperative conditions, it is sufficient.
No further <s>karma</s> can propel those who have transcended the craving for existence.
In the knowledge of suffering, [there flows] the stream of prior <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) that are not opposed [to liberation].
Compassion is an essential property (<s>vastudharma</s>) that arises [naturally]; it does not conform to [attachment to] beings.
<s>Rāga</s> (attachment) toward a <s>dharma</s> (phenomenon) that is not of that nature [arises] from the superimposition of another self.
Thus compassion arises merely from contact with the continuum of suffering.

children.text: mohaśca mūlaṃ doṣāṇāṃ sa ca sattvagraho vinā // Pramāṇav_1.198 //
children.translated_text: <s>Moha</s> (delusion) is the root of the afflictions, and that [delusion], without the grasping of a self (<s>sattvagraha</s>), [cannot exist].

children.text: tanādyahetau na dveṣo na doṣo 'taḥ kṛpā matā /
children.translated_text: Without that [self-grasping] and the like as a cause, there is no aversion, no affliction; therefore compassion (<s>kṛpā</s>) is considered [non-afflicted].
There is no non-liberation when prior <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) are exhausted, because of the non-reconnection with others.
Those whose <s>saṃskāras</s> remain with unexhausted potency—they are the faultless ones.

children.text: mandatvāt karuṇāyāśca na yatnaḥ sthāpane mahān // Pramāṇav_1.200 //
children.translated_text: And because their compassion is mild, the effort to establish [others in liberation] is not great.

children.text: tiṣṭhantyeva parādhīnā yeṣāṃ tu mahatī kṛpā /
children.translated_text: Those whose compassion is great remain [in the world], dependent on others.
Through the cessation of <s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s> (the view of the personal self), the very first [moment of] non-existence [of affliction] would occur.

children.text: mārge cet sahajāhānerna hānau vā bhavaḥ kutaḥ /
children.translated_text: If [you ask about] the <s>mārga</s> (path): [afflictions] that are innate are not eliminated [all at once]; or if they are not eliminated, whence is existence?

children.text: sukhī bhaveyaṃ duḥkhī vā mā bhūvamiti tṛṣyataḥ // Pramāṇav_1.202 //
children.translated_text: Of one who craves 'May I be happy, may I not be miserable,'
that very cognition 'I am' is itself the innate perception of a self (<s>sattvadarśana</s>).
For no one who does not perceive 'I' has affection for a self.
And without love for the self, one who desires happiness does not pursue [it].

children.text: duḥkhasyotpādahetutvaṃ bandho nityasya tat kutaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.204 //
children.translated_text: Being the cause of the arising of suffering is bondage; whence is that for a permanent [entity]?
Not being the cause of the arising of suffering is liberation; whence is that for a permanent [entity]?

children.text: anityatvena yo 'vācyaḥ sa heturna hi kasyacit // Pramāṇav_1.205 //
children.translated_text: That which cannot be described as impermanent is not the cause of anything whatsoever.
Bondage and liberation too are not in any way possible for [something] indescribable.

children.text: nityaṃ tamāhurvidvāṃso yaḥ svabhāvo na naśyati // Pramāṇav_1.206 //
children.translated_text: The wise call 'permanent' that whose essential nature does not perish.
Abandoning this pitiable view, let that [nature] therefore be called 'impermanent.'
The <s>mārga</s> (path) has been taught; through its practice, the <s>āśraya</s> (mental basis) is transformed.
If there are afflictions even in [what has become] one's own nature—like the path [itself], because of [the mind] not being all-pervasive.

children.text: viṣayagrahaṇaṃ dharmo vijñānasya yathāsti saḥ // Pramāṇav_1.208 //
children.translated_text: The apprehension of objects is the property of <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), just as it exists [in its nature];
it [the object] is grasped, and it is the progenitor of that [consciousness]—and [one thinks] 'as having an existing self.'
This is the natural disposition (<s>prakṛti</s>) of that [consciousness]; stumbling from that due to another occasion,
in the reversal [of error], it depends on conditions [and] is unsteady, like the cognition of a snake [in a rope].
This <s>citta</s> (mind) is luminous by nature (<s>prabhāsvara</s>); the defilements (<s>mala</s>) are adventitious (<s>āgantuka</s>).
Of those [defilements] that were previously incapable, whence comes the power later, when [the mind] is filled with that [luminosity]?
[Defilements] cannot sprout ultimately, like fire in moist ground that is flowing [with water].
Even in a thing that has the capacity, [when] the womb [of that capacity contains] the power for the arising of an antidote,
for one whose nature is the reality of undisturbed elemental truth,
there is no obstruction of cognition even when effort is applied, because of [cognition's] partiality toward that [truth].
Because [desire and aversion] have their single source in self-grasping (<s>ātmagraha</s>), through the relation of cause and effect,
the obstruction of <s>rāga</s> (desire) and <s>pratigha</s> (aversion) [occurs]; even in their difference, [they do] not [obstruct] each other.
Because <s>maitrī</s> (loving-kindness) and the like do not oppose <s>moha</s> (delusion), they do not ultimately restrain the afflictions.

children.text: tanmūlāśca malāḥ sarve sa ca satkāyadarśanam /
children.translated_text: All defilements are rooted in that [delusion], and that is <s>satkāyadarśana</s> (the view of the personal self).
Because <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) is the antidote, and because [the self-view] is apprehended as having this [false] nature,
false apprehension is <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance); and by reasoning, what is other [than correct knowledge] is unreasonable.

children.text: vyākhyeyo 'tra virodho yaḥ tadvirodhācca tanmayaiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.216 //
children.translated_text: The opposition that is to be explained here—and through opposition to that, by those who are composed of that [ignorance],
the opposition of the vision of <s>śūnyatā</s> (emptiness) to the afflictions of self[-grasping] is established.
[The objection:] there is no destruction, because [afflictions] are properties of living beings, like form and such—[this is] not established,
because of not observing the abandonment of the antidote's connection [with them], and also
there is no re-arising—like hardness—of what opposes the afflictions.

children.text: snehāt sukheṣu tṛṣyati tṛṣṇā doṣāṃstiraskurute // Pramāṇav_1.219 //
tenātmābhiniveśo yāvat tāvat sa saṃsāre // Pramāṇav_1.220 //
anayoḥ sampratibaddhāḥ sarve doṣāḥ prajāyante // Pramāṇav_1.221 //
snehaḥ sadoṣa iti cet tataḥ kiṃ tasya varjanam // Pramāṇav_1.223 //
adūṣite 'sya viṣaye na śakyaṃ tasya vajanam /
tayoradṛṣṭirviṣaye na tu bāhyeṣu yaḥ kramaḥ /
na hi snehaguṇāt snehaḥ kintvarthaguṇadarśanāt // Pramāṇav_1.225 //
kā vā sadoṣatā dṛṣṭā snehe duḥkhasamāśrayaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.226 //
na tairvinā duḥkhaheturātmā cet te 'pi tādṛśāḥ // Pramāṇav_1.227 //
svatvadhīḥ kena vāryeta vairāgyaṃ tatra tat kutaḥ /
sa tathaiveti sā doṣadṛṣṭāvapi na hīyate /
na h yekāntena tad duḥkhaṃ bhūyasā saviṣānnavat // Pramāṇav_1.233 //
alābhe mattakāsinyā dṛṣṭā tiryakṣu kāmitā // Pramāṇav_1.235 //
icchet prema katham premṇaḥ prakṛtirna hi tādṛśī /
pratyakṣaṃ pūrvamapi tat tathāpi na virāgavān /
yadyapyekatra doṣeṇa tatkṣaṇaṃ calitā matiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.241 //
nirdoṣaviṣayaḥ sneho nirdoṣaḥ sādhanāni ca // Pramāṇav_1.243 //
etāvadeva ca jagat kvedānīṃ sa virajyate /
sadoṣatāpi cet tasya tatrātmanyapi sā samā // Pramāṇav_1.244 //
sa cendriyādau na tvevaṃ bālāderapi sambhavāt /
tata eva ca nātmīyabuddherapi guṇekṣaṇam // Pramāṇav_1.247 //
api cāsadguṇāropaḥ snehāt tatra hi dṛśyate // Pramāṇav_1.248 //
tasmānnaikatvadṛṣṭyāpi snehaḥ snihyan sa ātmani // Pramāṇav_1.250 //
pratyutpannāt tu yo duḥkhānnirvedo dveṣa īdṛśaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.251 //
tasmin nivṛtte prakṛtiṃ svāmeva bhajate punaḥ /
sā ca naḥ pratyayotpattiḥ sā nairātmyadṛgāśrayaḥ /
ātmīyameva yo necched bhoktāpyasya na vidyate // Pramāṇav_1.257 //
ātmāpi na tadā tasya kriyābhogau hi lakṣaṇam /
prāg gurorlāghavāt paścānna pāpaharaṇaṃ kṛtam // Pramāṇav_1.261 //
mā bhūd gauravamevāsya na pāpaṃ gurvamūrttitaḥ /
tayoreva hi sāmarthya jātau tanmātrabhāvataḥ // Pramāṇav_1.263 //
dṛṣṭaṃ buddherna cānyasya santi tāni nayanti kim /
atha buddhestadābhāvānna syuḥ sandhīyate malaiḥ // Pramāṇav_1.267 //
kṛrtṛ bhoktṛtvahāniḥ syāt sāmarthya ca na sidhyati /
asambhavād vipakṣasya na hāniḥ karmadehayo // Pramāṇav_1.275 //
dvayakṣayārtha yatne ca vyarthaḥ karmakṣaye śramaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.276 //
karmaṇāṃ tāpasaṃkleśāt naikarūpāt tataḥ kṣayaḥ // Pramāṇav_1.277 //
yadīṣṭamaparaṃ kleśāt tat tapaḥ kleśa eva cet // Pramāṇav_1.279 //
tajje karmaṇi śaktāḥ syuḥ kṛtihāniḥ kathaṃ bhavet /
doṣā na karmaṇo duṣṭaḥ karoti na viparyayāt // Pramāṇav_1.281 //
dayayā śreya ācaṣṭe jñānāt satyaṃ sasādhanam // Pramāṇav_1.284 //
anyat saṃvṛtaisat proktam te svasāmānyalakṣaṇe // Pramāṇav_2.3 //
children.translated_text: What is other [than that] is declared to be conventionally unreal; those two are the own-characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) and the general-characteristic (<s>sāmānyalakṣaṇa</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.3 //
If [you say] everything is incapable — [we reply:] in the case of seeds and the like with respect to sprouts and the like,

children.text: dṛṣṭā śaktiḥ matā sā cet saṃvṛtyā astu yathā tathā // Pramāṇav_2.4 //
children.translated_text: a capacity is observed. If you accept that, let it exist conventionally, in whatever manner. // Pramāṇav 2.4 //
If [you say] that [capacity] exists everywhere — [we reply:] since there is no [universal] positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>) of cognition,
because the general-characteristic is not observed — like the cognition of form and the like from the eye. // Pramāṇav 2.5 //
By this, [the cognitions] arising from conventional usage (<s>samayābhoga</s>) and the like, from the influence of internal [factors],
the cognitions regarding pot-lifting, generality, number, and the like are explained. // Pramāṇav 2.6 //
Hair and the like are not a universal — because of attachment to what is non-beneficial;

children.text: jñeyatvena grahād doṣo nabhāveṣu prasajyate // Pramāṇav_2.7 //
children.translated_text: the fault does not apply to non-existents, since they are grasped [only] as 'objects of knowledge.' // Pramāṇav 2.7 //
Even regarding those [non-existents], since the same nature holds and there is no prohibition, they have evident appearance;
but the cognition 'hair and the like' is [caused] by the fact that being in the form of cognition constitutes being an object. // Pramāṇav 2.8 //
The appearance of hair, which has a universal as its object, is meaningless;
if being in the form of cognition constitutes being an object, then the [same] consequence would apply to the universal. // Pramāṇav 2.9 //
Since that is accepted, there is no fault; the sameness is by virtue of having the form of an object;
because of having the same form everywhere, and because of depending on the exclusion from that [other]. // Pramāṇav 2.10 //
That [universal] does not [exist independently], because the real thing (<s>vastu</s>) is not to be expressed; because of the effectiveness of the collection of sense-faculties,
in the utterance of names and the like, which is connected with the speaker, the hearer, and the denotatum. // Pramāṇav 2.11 //
If names and the like are unconnected [with objects], there would be no activity regarding the object;

children.text: sārūpyād bhrāntito vṛttirarthecet syānna sarvadā // Pramāṇav_2.12 //
children.translated_text: if activity [occurs] regarding the object through similarity, due to error — then it would not [occur] always. // Pramāṇav 2.12 //
And spatial error does not [apply] to cognition — since the cognitions arise equally,
and because a cognition of that kind does not subside when [one is] elsewhere. // Pramāṇav 2.13 //
Or the invalidity of the means [of knowledge] for the cognition that has the appearance of an external object,
because the separateness of [something] distinct from consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is not established. // Pramāṇav 2.14 //
If [you say] all cognitions have objects — [we reply:] since in dreams and the like there is perception of what is otherwise,
that is improper. And it is not from latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), because there is the appearance of blue and the like. // Pramāṇav 2.15 //
Since there is no obstruction of blue and the like, the cognition is not [produced] by those qualified to [present] the appropriate location;

children.text: ajñātasya svayaṃ jñānāt nāmādyetena varṇitam // Pramāṇav_2.16 //
children.translated_text: since what is unknown is known by itself — names and the like are explained by this. // Pramāṇav 2.16 //
That alone is held to have a [real] object. By what is the cognition from the eye and the like considered [valid]?
If because of the observed capacity of the object — [then] what is obtained otherwise is purposeless. // Pramāṇav 2.17 //
If activity would occur even in the absence of connection, just as if there were connection with the object —

children.text: atītānāgataṃ vācyaṃ na syādarthena tatkṣayāt // Pramāṇav_2.18 //
children.translated_text: then the past and the future could be expressed, but that is not so, because of [their] destruction. // Pramāṇav 2.18 //
If [you think] there is no undesirable consequence because words apprehend a universal —
that is not so, because the bare universal alone is not apprehended; or even if it is apprehended, // Pramāṇav 2.19 //
the individuals are not identical with that universal; therefore there would be eternal apprehension;

children.text: nityatvācca yadi vyaktirvyakteḥ pratyakṣatāṃ prati // Pramāṇav_2.20 //
children.translated_text: and if the individual is eternal — with regard to the perceptibility of the individual: // Pramāṇav 2.20 //
whatever is capable of producing cognition in itself — that is capable indeed;
but if sometimes incapable — then it would be incapable always. // Pramāṇav 2.21 //
Whether its capacity or incapacity is established by its own nature —

children.text: nityatvādapi kiṃ tasya kastāṃ kṣapayituṃ kṣamaḥ // Pramāṇav_2.22 //
children.translated_text: since it is eternal, what of it? Who is capable of destroying it? // Pramāṇav 2.22 //
And that cognition of the universal, when examined in conformity [with the facts], is found [to contain] —

children.text: nīlādyākāraleśo yaḥ sa tasmin kena nirmitaḥ // Pramāṇav_2.23 //
children.translated_text: a trace of the form of blue and the like. Who has produced that [trace] in it? // Pramāṇav 2.23 //
If [you say] the sense-faculties are not purposeless because they serve the purpose of perceptual cognition —
then how does that very cognition, having a single form, appear as differentiated from words and the like? // Pramāṇav 2.24 //
It is not the universal, nor the individual possessing the universal, [nor] form, by which something dependent on another

children.text: siddham pṛthak cet kāryatvaṃ hyapekṣetyabhidhīyate // Pramāṇav_2.25 //
children.translated_text: is established. If [you say it is] separate — then it is said to require effectedness (<s>kāryatva</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.25 //
Even what is independent in its production is an effect from its own cause;
it is connected through conceptual construction — how could there be something that is in no way an effect? // Pramāṇav 2.26 //
If [they are] different, that [universal] is unconnected [with the particular]; the established [conclusion] is the absence of own-nature (<s>niḥsvabhāvatā</s>);
the consequence of a universal for a non-existent [follows]; and since there is no mutual dependence between those two. // Pramāṇav 2.27 //
Therefore, the universal, being formless, is not established as a substrate of forms;
the universal (<s>jāti</s>) is revealed by words that serve to apprehend the distinctions of that. // Pramāṇav 2.28 //
Whatever appearance of form there is in that [universal], or the grasping of the object as real —
that is error (<s>bhrānti</s>), produced by the habituation of seeing from beginningless time. // Pramāṇav 2.29 //
And that commonality (<s>sāmānya</s>) of objects which is characterized by exclusion from others (<s>anyavyāvṛtti</s>) —

children.text: yanniṣṭhāsta ime śabdā na rūpaṃ tasya kiñcana // Pramāṇav_2.30 //
children.translated_text: in which these words are grounded — that has no form whatsoever. // Pramāṇav 2.30 //
Since in the cognition of the universal, the universal being formless is not observed [directly],
even the error regarding the object would be [accepted]; the universal too is [accepted], because of the flow [of conceptual thought]. // Pramāṇav 2.31 //
Because in reality it does not exist as having the form of an object, it is not something with form;
because of having no own-nature, [the universal] is inexpressible — [yet] from some utterance, [there is] a notion. // Pramāṇav 2.32 //
If the inexpressibility of real things regarding real things is [maintained] in some way —
it should not be expressed at all; because of the difference of substrata, [expression is] through figurative usage of difference. // Pramāṇav 2.33 //
Even regarding past and future objects, verbal usages grounded in the universal

children.text: śrutayo niviśante sadasaddharmaḥ kathaṃ bhavet // Pramāṇav_2.34 //
children.translated_text: apply — how can [the universal] have the property of being both existent and non-existent? // Pramāṇav 2.34 //
If [you say] that is through figurative usage — what is the proximity of a presently existing pot

children.text: pratyāsattirabhāvena yā paṭādau na vidyate // Pramāṇav_2.35 //
children.translated_text: through non-existence, which is not found in cloth and the like? // Pramāṇav 2.35 //
The unerring operation of cognition is always [present] in the primary and the imposed senses;

children.text: siṃhe māṇavake tadvad ghoṣaṇāpyasti laukikī // Pramāṇav_2.36 //
children.translated_text: just as with a lion and a young man — there is also worldly proclamation. // Pramāṇav 2.36 //
Where, through convention (<s>rūḍhi</s>), a word is applied by people even to a false object —

children.text: sa mukhyastatra tatsāmyādū gauṇo 'nyatra skhaladgatiḥ // Pramāṇav_2.37 //
children.translated_text: that is its primary [sense] there; the secondary (<s>gauṇa</s>) [sense], applied elsewhere through similarity, has an uncertain operation. // Pramāṇav 2.37 //
Just as, even regarding [what has] existence, one might apply the designation of non-existence, or make a fabrication;

children.text: kuryādaśakte śakte vā pradhānādiśrutiṃ janaḥ // Pramāṇav_2.38 //
children.translated_text: or apply to what is incapable or capable the verbal usage '<s>pradhāna</s>' (primordial matter) and the like. // Pramāṇav 2.38 //
Whatever cognition arises from words is seen whether [the object] has perished or has not perished —
such alone is [the cognition] of objects that [truly] exist; this is not [the nature] of the cognitions from the ear and other [senses]. // Pramāṇav 2.39 //
If [you say] both cognitions [verbal and sensory] have a universal as [their] content, because of grasping the universal alone —

children.text: tasyāpi kevalasya prāg grahaṇaṃ vinivāritam // Pramāṇav_2.40 //
children.translated_text: the grasping of that [universal] by itself alone has already been refuted earlier. // Pramāṇav 2.40 //
How can what is undifferentiated belong to [things] mutually differentiated?

children.text: tathā dvirūpatāyāṃ vā tad vastvekaṃ kathaṃ bhavet // Pramāṇav_2.41 //
children.translated_text: Or if there is a dual nature, how can that reality be one? // Pramāṇav 2.41 //

children.text: tābhyāṃ tadanyadeva syād yadi rūpaṃ samaṃ tayoḥ /
children.translated_text: If it is other than both of those, and the form is the same for both —

children.text: tayoriti na sambandho vyāvṛttistu na duṣyati // Pramāṇav_2.42 //
children.translated_text: the relation 'of those two' does not hold; but exclusion (<s>vyāvṛtti</s>) is not contradicted. // Pramāṇav 2.42 //
Therefore, the very sameness in this [so-called] universal is a characteristic of what is unreal (<s>avastu</s>);

children.text: kārya cet tadanekaṃ syānnaścaraṃ ca na tanmatam // Pramāṇav_2.43 //
children.translated_text: if [it were] an effect, it would be many; and if transient — that is not your view. // Pramāṇav 2.43 //
Because destruction follows mere existence, there is no permanence;
and because universals are unconnected [with particulars], [and] because they are not effects, [they are] formless. // Pramāṇav 2.44 //
And that cognition which arises by the force of the object depends on [the object];

children.text: na saṃketa sa sāmānyabuddhuṣvetad vibhāvyate // Pramāṇav_2.45 //
children.translated_text: it does not [depend on] convention — this is to be understood in cognitions of the universal. // Pramāṇav 2.45 //
And whatever cognition follows non-difference upon observing two objects —
that, without convention, is based on proximity to a [real] object. // Pramāṇav 2.46 //
The proximity [to objects] without universals, as accepted [by us], is like [the cognition] from the eye and the like;
or how does the universal conform to the effects of cognition, through division? // Pramāṇav 2.47 //
Even though to some extent [there is content] in cognition, since the form of that does not appear —

children.text: yadi nāmendriyāṇāṃ syād draṣṭā bhāseta tadvapuḥ // Pramāṇav_2.48 //
children.translated_text: if [the universal] were of the nature of the sense-faculties, the seer would appear in that form. // Pramāṇav 2.48 //
Because [universals] have form, [yet] because bare universals alone are not observed —
and in the grasping of the individual, nothing other than word-form and the like is seen. // Pramāṇav 2.49 //

body.text:
jñānamātrārthakaraṇe 'pyayogyamata eva tat /
tadayogyatayārūpaṃ taddhyavastuṣu lakṣaṇam // Pramāṇav_2.50 // Pramāṇav_2.//
body.translated_text:
Even for the purpose of merely producing a cognition of the object, it [the universal] is unfit — precisely for that reason;
because of that unfitness, it is formless — for that indeed is the mark of [what pertains to] real things. // Pramāṇav 2.50 //

children.translated_text: What is the opposite of what has been stated — that is accepted as the own-characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>);
and the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is threefold, based on the existent, the non-existent, and both. // Pramāṇav 2.51 //
If the cognition based on the existent [is considered, then] because the existent is connected with [another] existent,
there is no [need for further] reply [since it is] already answered; because it is observed; and [it applies] otherwise regarding the past and the like. // Pramāṇav 2.52 //
If [you object that] there is loss of being a property of the existent — [we reply:] since that cognition
is preceded by the grasping of the existent, there is no fault in this; but the object of measurement is one — the own-characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.53 //
Therefore, since causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>) is established, and since the investigation of existence and non-existence [depends on it],
because of the apprehension of that [object] through its own form and through another's form, a twofold object of knowledge is accepted. // Pramāṇav 2.54 //
The second [mode of apprehension], through inappropriate fixation, is accepted as error (<s>bhrānti</s>);

children.text: gatiścet pararūpeṇa na ca bhrānteḥ pramāṇatā // Pramāṇav_2.55 //
children.translated_text: if [you say] the apprehension is through another's form — but error has no validity as a means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.55 //
Even error has validity as a means of knowledge, because of non-deception regarding the intended [purpose];
and apprehension has also been observed otherwise; and this position has already been answered. // Pramāṇav 2.56 //
For one who runs toward the light of a gem and the light of a lamp with the cognition 'gem!' —
even though the two erroneous cognitions are indistinguishable, there is a distinction with regard to causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.57 //
Just so, even though both [perception and inference] are non-veridical in the same way,
their validity as means of knowledge is established in accordance with causal efficacy. // Pramāṇav 2.58 //
The cognition which, by the force of the object, possesses positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvayavyatireka</s>) —
the grasping of that [object] is by itself; therefore the other [kind of] object is beyond the senses (<s>atīndriya</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.59 //
For that [object] whose own form is not seen, another object is the basis of [its] apprehension;

children.text: tadāśrayeṇa sambandhī yadi syād gamakastadā // Pramāṇav_2.60 //
children.translated_text: if [something] connected through that basis exists — then it is an indicator (<s>gamaka</s>). // Pramāṇav 2.60 //
At that time, apprehension [occurs] only through the general form that follows the indicator;

children.text: tasmāt sarvaḥ parokṣo 'rtho viśeṣeṇa na gamyate // Pramāṇav_2.61 //
children.translated_text: therefore, every imperceptible object is not known in its particularity. // Pramāṇav 2.61 //

children.text: yā ca sambandhino dharmād bhūtirdharmiṇi jñāyate /
children.translated_text: And the existence of a property-possessor (<s>dharmin</s>) that is known from the property (<s>dharma</s>) of something connected —
that is inference (<s>anumāna</s>), exclusively the means of establishing imperceptible [objects]. // Pramāṇav 2.62 //
There is no possibility of another [kind of] object of knowledge through perception and inference;
therefore, from the twofold nature of the object of knowledge, a twofold means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) is accepted. // Pramāṇav 2.63 //
Or, the refutation of [the numbers] three and one [as counts of pramāṇas] is [established] from seeing the twofold nature of the object of knowledge;
if [you say the object is] one alone — because the non-existent is not an object of knowledge — that is [also] our position. // Pramāṇav 2.64 //
If [you say] there is indefiniteness regarding the non-existence being an object of knowledge — [we reply:] the ascertainment of non-existence [is needed];

children.text: tanniścyapramāraṇaṃ vā dvitīyam nākṣajā matiḥ // Pramāṇav_2.65 //
children.translated_text: or a second means of knowledge for that ascertainment — and it is not a sense-born cognition. // Pramāṇav 2.65 //
If in the absence [of an object], cognition were born from the force of the object, without depending on the object's capacity,
then even when there are obstructions and the like, sense-born cognition would arise. // Pramāṇav 2.66 //
If [you say] there is cessation in the absence [of the object] — that is precisely the determination of perception;
or that [cessation] itself is a contradictory mark (<s>liṅga</s>), possessing positive and negative concomitance. // Pramāṇav 2.67 //
And the twofold means of knowledge is established from the ascertainment of another's consciousness;
